Fragmented government data undermines India’s AI ambitions: Report Poor quality data causes fiscal leakage equivalent to 4–7% of India’s annual welfare spending, the report said By BL Mumbai Bureau Updated - October 16, 2026 at 06:14 AM. | Mumbai, October 9 × Share WhatsApp X Facebook LinkedIn Messenger Reddit Mail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/info-tech/fragmented-government-data-undermines-indias-ai-ambitions-report/article71564146.ece Copy The report states removing 17.1 million ineligible beneficiaries from the PM-KISAN farmer support scheme saved an estimated ₹9,000 crore, while eliminating 35 million bogus LPG connections saved ₹21,000 crore over two years | Photo Credit: Kavithaa Sri R _12192 Fragmented government data across departments and states is hampering public-service delivery and could undermine India’s artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions, requiring states to establish common data standards and stronger quality controls, according to a report by the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. The report estimates that poor quality data causes fiscal leakage equivalent to 4–7 per cent of India’s annual welfare spending, citing a 2025 NITI Aayog assessment. While India has built digital infrastructure at an unprecedented scale, government data remains siloed, with departments collecting information primarily to meet their individual reporting requirements rather than support cross-sector policy decisions, said the report titled 'From Digital Scale to Data Power: A Data Operating Model for India’s States’. Removing 17.1 million ineligible beneficiaries from the PM-KISAN farmer support scheme saved an estimated ₹9,000 crore, while eliminating 35 million bogus LPG connections saved ₹21,000 crore over two years. Removing 16 million fake ration cards is saving about ₹10,000 crore annually, the report said. The report recommended a State-level data operating model covering leadership and institutional mandates, data ownership and stewardship, common standards, shared data capabilities, independent quality assurance, legal and procurement safeguards, and a State Data Balance Sheet to track data assets and associated risks. Vivek Agarwal, Country Director, TBI, and co-author said states that are establishing sound data foundations would be better equipped to improve decisions and deliver public services faster. India’s digital infrastructure includes Aadhaar, which has enrolled more than 1.4 billion people, and the Unified Payments Interface, which processes over 20 billion transactions a month. DigiLocker has issued and verified nearly 10 billion documents for more than 685 million citizens. However, digital scale does not automatically make data interoperable across departments, the report said. Ott Velsberg, former Government Chief Data Officer of Estonia and co-author, said connecting and improving the reliability of government data would be critical to translating digital infrastructure into better public outcomes. Without these foundations, AI could amplify existing gaps in government information rather than resolve them, the report cautioned, he said.
